claim: MMP14 is a potent pericellular collagenase that can cleave type I collagen in vitro.
source: MMP14 is a potent pericellular collagenase that can cleave type I collagen in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about MMP14's enzymatic activity.

claim: Tendon development is arrested in Scleraxis-Cre::Mmp14 lox/lox mice that are unable to release collagen fibrils from plasma membrane fibripositors.
source: In this study, we show that tendon development is arrested in Scleraxis-Cre::Mmp14 lox/lox mice that are unable to release collagen fibrils from plasma membrane fibripositors.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: MMP14 promotes embryonic tissue formation by releasing collagen fibrils from the cell surface.
source: In contrast to its role in collagen turnover in adult tissue, MMP14 promotes embryonic tissue formation by releasing collagen fibrils from the cell surface.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Tendons grow to normal size in Col-r/r mice that have a mutated collagen-I that is uncleavable by MMPs.
source: Notably, the tendons grow to normal size and collagen fibril release from fibripositors occurs in Col-r/r mice that have a mutated collagen-I that is uncleavable by MMPs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data comparing Col-r/r and WT mice.

claim: Collagen fibril release from fibripositors occurs in Col-r/r mice that have a mutated collagen-I that is uncleavable by MMPs.
source: Notably, the tendons grow to normal size and collagen fibril release from fibripositors occurs in Col-r/r mice that have a mutated collagen-I that is uncleavable by MMPs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations.

claim: Fibronectin (not collagen-I) accumulates in the tendons of Mmp14-null mice.
source: Furthermore, fibronectin (not collagen-I) accumulates in the tendons of Mmp14-null mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by mass spectrometry and immunofluorescence data.

claim: MMP14 cleaves a molecular bridge tethering collagen fibrils to the plasma membrane of fibripositors.
source: We propose a model for cell-regulated collagen fibril assembly during tendon development in which MMP14 cleaves a molecular bridge tethering collagen fibrils to the plasma membrane of fibripositors.
evidence: This is a proposed model stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: MMP14 contains a transmembrane domain for insertion into the plasma membrane.
source: Matrix metalloproteinase 14 (MMP14, also known as membrane type I-MMP) is a member of the family of MMPs and contains a transmembrane domain for insertion into the plasma membrane (Sato et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sato et al., 1994.

claim: MMP14 has been implicated in cancer cell invasion.
source: MMP14 has been implicated in cancer cell invasion (Hotary et al., 2003) and embryonic development (Holmbeck et al., 1999; Zhou et al., 2000) because of its ability to degrade extracellular matrix (ECM) macromolecules especially type I collagen (Overall, 2001; Tam et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2006; Kessenbrock et al., 2010; Gialeli et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hotary et al., 2003.

claim: MMP14 has been implicated in embryonic development.
source: MMP14 has been implicated in cancer cell invasion (Hotary et al., 2003) and embryonic development (Holmbeck et al., 1999; Zhou et al., 2000) because of its ability to degrade extracellular matrix (ECM) macromolecules especially type I collagen (Overall, 2001; Tam et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2006; Kessenbrock et al., 2010; Gialeli et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Holmbeck et al., 1999 and Zhou et al., 2000.

claim: Mice deficient in MMP14 die within a few weeks of birth with generalized connective tissue abnormalities including osteopenia and soft tissue frailty.
source: Mice deficient in MMP14 die within a few weeks of birth with generalized connective tissue abnormalities including osteopenia and soft tissue frailty (Holmbeck et al., 1999; Zhou et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Holmbeck et al., 1999 and Zhou et al., 2000.

claim: More than 28 collagen and collagen-related proteins occur in vertebrate tissues.
source: More than 28 collagen and collagen-related proteins occur in vertebrate tissues of which type I collagen is the archetypal member of the subfamily of fibril-forming collagens (Kadler et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kadler et al., 2007.

claim: Type I collagen is the archetypal member of the subfamily of fibril-forming collagens.
source: More than 28 collagen and collagen-related proteins occur in vertebrate tissues of which type I collagen is the archetypal member of the subfamily of fibril-forming collagens (Kadler et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kadler et al., 2007.

claim: Collagen fibrils formed from type I collagen have a mass per unit length up to approximately 0.3 TDa/µm.
source: The fibrils formed from type I collagen are the largest (with a mass per unit length up to ∼0.3 TDa/µm) and most size pleomorphic (from ∼1 µm to >1 mm) protein polymers in vertebrates and are essential for fibrous tissue development (Schnieke et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schnieke et al., 1983.

claim: Collagen fibrils are the most size pleomorphic protein polymers in vertebrates, ranging from approximately 1 µm to greater than 1 mm.
source: The fibrils formed from type I collagen are the largest (with a mass per unit length up to ∼0.3 TDa/µm) and most size pleomorphic (from ∼1 µm to >1 mm) protein polymers in vertebrates and are essential for fibrous tissue development (Schnieke et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schnieke et al., 1983.

claim: Collagen fibrils are essential for fibrous tissue development.
source: The fibrils formed from type I collagen are the largest (with a mass per unit length up to ∼0.3 TDa/µm) and most size pleomorphic (from ∼1 µm to >1 mm) protein polymers in vertebrates and are essential for fibrous tissue development (Schnieke et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schnieke et al., 1983.

claim: Embryonic tendon contains narrow diameter (approximately 50 nm) fibrils.
source: Collagen fibril assembly has best been studied in embryonic tendon, which contains narrow diameter (∼50 nm) fibrils in which one end of the fibril is located within actin-dependent (Canty et al., 2006) invaginations of the plasma membrane called fibripositors (Canty et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Canty et al., 2006 and Canty et al., 2004.

claim: One end of the fibril is located within actin-dependent invaginations of the plasma membrane called fibripositors.
source: Collagen fibril assembly has best been studied in embryonic tendon, which contains narrow diameter (∼50 nm) fibrils in which one end of the fibril is located within actin-dependent (Canty et al., 2006) invaginations of the plasma membrane called fibripositors (Canty et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Canty et al., 2006 and Canty et al., 2004.

claim: Fibripositors are points of fibril assembly and sites of attachment of the cell to the ECM.
source: Fibripositors are points of fibril assembly and sites of attachment of the cell to the ECM (Kalson et al., 2013) and exhibit a range of morphologies depending on the presence or absence of a slender finger-like projection of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kalson et al., 2013.

claim: Protruding fibripositors exhibit the invagination and the finger-like projection whereas recessed fibripositors only exhibit the invagination.
source: Protruding fibripositors exhibit the invagination and the finger-like projection whereas recessed fibripositors only exhibit the invagination (Kalson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kalson et al., 2013.

claim: The transport of collagen fibrils into fibripositors is powered by non-muscle myosin II.
source: The transport of collagen fibrils into fibripositors is powered by non-muscle myosin II and is not part of a fibril degradation process in embryonic tendon (Kalson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kalson et al., 2013.

claim: The transport of collagen fibrils into fibripositors is not part of a fibril degradation process in embryonic tendon.
source: The transport of collagen fibrils into fibripositors is powered by non-muscle myosin II and is not part of a fibril degradation process in embryonic tendon (Kalson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kalson et al., 2013.

claim: Short collagen fibrils can be found within membrane-sealed compartments termed fibricarriers.
source: Short collagen fibrils can be found within membrane-sealed compartments termed fibricarriers (Canty et al., 2004; Kalson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Canty et al., 2004 and Kalson et al., 2013.

claim: Embryonic tendon transitions from a unimodal distribution of narrow (approximately 50 nm) diameter collagen fibrils to a bimodal distribution in adult tissues with means of approximately 50 nm and approximately 200 nm diameter fibrils.
source: The transition from a unimodal distribution of narrow (∼50 nm) diameter collagen fibrils in embryonic tendon to a bimodal distribution in adult tissues with means of ∼50 nm and ∼200 nm diameter fibrils is a fascinating phenomenon (Parry et al., 1978; Derwin and Soslowsky, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Parry et al., 1978 and Derwin and Soslowsky, 1999.

claim: Stage 1 of tendon development occurs during E14.5 to birth (in mice) and is characterized by narrow-diameter collagen fibrils in fibripositors during which fibril number is determined.
source: The presence of narrow-diameter collagen fibrils in fibripositors during E14.5 to birth (in mice) signifies stage 1 of tendon development during which fibril number is determined (Kalson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kalson et al., 2015.

claim: Stage 2 of tendon development occurs soon after birth (in mice) and is characterized by the disappearance of fibripositors, the release of fibrils to the ECM and the growth of fibrils in length and diameter.
source: Stage 2 occurs soon after birth (in mice) and is characterized by the disappearance of fibripositors, the release of fibrils to the ECM and the growth of fibrils in length and diameter (Kalson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kalson et al., 2015.

claim: In the absence of MMP14, progression from stage 1 to stage 2 does not occur.
source: We show here that in the absence of MMP14, progression from stage 1–2 does not occur, fibrils are retained by fibripositors, fibril diameters keep to ∼50 nm, and tendon development stops at stage 1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data.

claim: In the absence of MMP14, fibrils are retained by fibripositors.
source: We show here that in the absence of MMP14, progression from stage 1–2 does not occur, fibrils are retained by fibripositors, fibril diameters keep to ∼50 nm, and tendon development stops at stage 1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data.

claim: In the absence of MMP14, fibril diameters remain at approximately 50 nm.
source: We show here that in the absence of MMP14, progression from stage 1–2 does not occur, fibrils are retained by fibripositors, fibril diameters keep to ∼50 nm, and tendon development stops at stage 1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data.

claim: In the absence of MMP14, tendon development stops at stage 1.
source: We show here that in the absence of MMP14, progression from stage 1–2 does not occur, fibrils are retained by fibripositors, fibril diameters keep to ∼50 nm, and tendon development stops at stage 1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data.

claim: Wild type and Mmp14 knockout littermates had similar birth weights.
source: Wild type (WT) and Mmp14 knockout (KO) littermates had similar birth weights but the KO mice were growth retarded at 3 days after birth (P3) (Figure 1A, as reported previously [Holmbeck et al., 1999]).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A, with citation to Holmbeck et al., 1999.

claim: Mmp14 knockout mice were growth retarded at 3 days after birth (P3).
source: Wild type (WT) and Mmp14 knockout (KO) littermates had similar birth weights but the KO mice were growth retarded at 3 days after birth (P3) (Figure 1A, as reported previously [Holmbeck et al., 1999]).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A, with citation to Holmbeck et al., 1999.

claim: The tendons of Mmp14 KO mice at P0 were thinner than those of WT mice.
source: Morphometric analyses at P0 showed that the tendons of the KO mice were thinner than those of WT mice (Figure 1B) and had fewer bundles of fibrils (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mmp14 KO tendons at P0 had fewer bundles of fibrils than WT tendons.
source: Morphometric analyses at P0 showed that the tendons of the KO mice were thinner than those of WT mice (Figure 1B) and had fewer bundles of fibrils (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: In transverse section, Mmp14 KO tendons had fewer fibrils that were organized into fewer and irregular bundles.
source: In transverse section, Mmp14 KO tendons had fewer fibrils that were organized into fewer and irregular bundles (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: There was no difference in the number of cells per unit volume of the tendon between WT and Mmp14 KO tendon.
source: We detected no difference in the number of cells per unit volume of the tendon between WT and Mmp14 KO tendon (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: There was no difference in fibril volume fraction (FVF) between WT and Mmp14 KO tendons at P0.
source: There was no difference in fibril volume fraction (FVF) (Figure 1D); therefore, there was no evidence of abnormal fibril–fibril interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There was no evidence of abnormal fibril–fibril interactions in Mmp14 KO tendons.
source: There was no difference in fibril volume fraction (FVF) (Figure 1D); therefore, there was no evidence of abnormal fibril–fibril interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the FVF data.

claim: Mmp14 KO tendons were mechanically weaker than WT tendon.
source: Mmp14 KO tendons were mechanically weaker than WT tendon (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: After adjustment for size, the Mmp14 KO tendons had similar mechanical properties to those of tendons from WT animals.
source: However, after adjustment for size, the KO tendons had similar mechanical properties to those of tendons from WT animals, which was consistent with the normal FVF.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There were no differences in Col1a1 gene expression at P0 between WT and Mmp14 KO tendons.
source: Quantitative PCR analysis showed no differences in Col1a1 gene expression at P0 (Figure 1F) and [14C]-proline labeling showed that procollagen processing was unaffected by loss of MMP14 (at P7, Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Procollagen processing was unaffected by loss of MMP14 at P7.
source: Quantitative PCR analysis showed no differences in Col1a1 gene expression at P0 (Figure 1F) and [14C]-proline labeling showed that procollagen processing was unaffected by loss of MMP14 (at P7, Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Despite no differences in gene expression or procollagen processing with MMP14 deficiency, there was decreased collagen synthesis in KO samples compared to WT animals.
source: However, despite no differences in gene expression or procollagen processing with MMP14 deficiency we found decreased collagen synthesis in KO samples, compared to WT animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The collagen fibril diameters in P0 Mmp14 KO mouse-tail tendon were significantly larger (by approximately 12%) than those in WT mice.
source: We next analyzed collagen fibril diameters. As shown in Figure 1H, the diameters in P0 KO mouse-tail tendon were significantly larger (by ∼12%) than those in WT mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1H.

claim: E15.5 WT tendons contained collagen fibrils in the ECM and a small number of collagen fibrils in fibripositors.
source: TEM analysis showed E15.5 WT tendons contained collagen fibrils in the ECM and a small number of collagen fibrils in fibripositors (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mmp14 KO tendons at E15.5 contained conspicuous electron-lucent invaginations characteristic of recessed fibripositors.
source: In contrast, Mmp14 KO tendons contained conspicuous electron-lucent invaginations characteristic of recessed fibripositors (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There were approximately 8 times the number of fibripositor cross-sections per nucleus in KO tenocytes compared to WT.
source: There were ∼8 times the number of fibripositor cross-sections per nucleus in KO tenocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Tracing of fibrils in 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM and electron tomography showed the presence of deep recessed fibripositors in Mmp14 KO cells with looped collagen fibrils.
source: Tracing of fibrils in 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM and electron tomography (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D) showed the presence of deep recessed fibripositors in Mmp14 KO cells (Videos 1, 2, respectively) with looped collagen fibrils.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D and Videos 1, 2.

claim: EM analysis of embryonic Mmp2 KO and Mmp13 KO tail tendons showed no obvious changes to fibripositor occurrence.
source: However, EM analysis of embryonic Mmp2 KO and Mmp13 KO tail tendons showed no obvious changes to fibripositor occurrence (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: WT tendon at E15.5 contained numerous fibril tips and short fibrils.
source: WT tendon contained numerous fibril tips and short fibrils (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Fibril tips were less frequent in KO tendon at E15.5 compared to WT.
source: In contrast, fibril tips were less frequent in KO tendon (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The average fibril length in E15.5 WT tendon was 16 ± 3 μm.
source: The average fibril length in E15.5 WT tendon was 16 ± 3 μm whereas that in an age-matched and anatomical-site-matched Mmp14 KO tendon was 38 ± 6 μm (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The average fibril length in E15.5 Mmp14 KO tendon was 38 ± 6 μm.
source: The average fibril length in E15.5 WT tendon was 16 ± 3 μm whereas that in an age-matched and anatomical-site-matched Mmp14 KO tendon was 38 ± 6 μm (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At E15.5, the tendon cross-sectional area and the FVF in WT and KO samples were not significantly different.
source: At E15.5, the tendon cross-sectional area and the FVF in WT and KO samples were not significantly different (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Given the same transverse area occupied by collagen fibrils in WT and KO tissue at E15.5, the difference in collagen mean fibril length equates to a approximately 2.5-fold reduction in fibril number in KO tendon.
source: Therefore, given the same transverse area occupied by collagen fibrils in WT and KO tissue, the difference in collagen mean fibril length equates to a ∼2.5-fold reduction in fibril number in KO tendon.
evidence: This is inferred from the fibril length and cross-sectional area data.

claim: At E16.5, fibrils were, on average, shorter in WT tendon (mean length 50 ± 9 μm) than KO tendon (mean length 111 ± 26 μm).
source: Analysis at E16.5 confirmed that fibrils were, on average, shorter in WT tendon than KO tendon (mean length 50 ± 9 μm) compared with 111 ± 26 μm (n = 668 WT fibrils, 683 KO fibrils, respectively, each tracked over 10 μm).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of fibril tracking data.

claim: The addition of GM6001 to tendon-like constructs recapitulated the fibripositor phenotype of the Mmp14-deficient mouse.
source: The addition of GM6001 to tendon-like constructs recapitulated the fibripositor phenotype of the Mmp14-deficient mouse (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: The catalytic activity of MMP14 is required for normal collagen fibril transport at fibripositors.
source: This indicated that the catalytic activity of MMP14 is required for normal collagen fibril transport at fibripositors.
evidence: This is inferred from the GM6001 inhibition experiment.

claim: Inhibition of MMPs resulted in increased mean fibril length in tendon-like constructs.
source: Estimation of collagen mean fibril lengths in the constructs showed that inhibition of MMPs resulted in increased mean fibril length (Figure 3G), as was observed in embryonic Mmp14 KO tendon.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The mean length of fibrils in WT and Mmp14 KO was the same in P0 tendons.
source: SBF-SEM analysis showed that the mean length of fibrils in WT and Mmp14 KO was the same in P0 tendons (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The more abundant but shorter fibrils in WT tendon grow in length during later embryonic development so that at P0 the fibrils are of equal mean length but there are more fibrils in the WT tendon than in Mmp14 KO tendon.
source: Therefore, the more abundant but shorter fibrils in WT tendon grow in length during later embryonic development so that at P0 the fibrils are of equal mean length but there are more fibrils in the WT tendon than in Mmp14 KO tendon.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of fibril lengths at E15.5 and P0.

claim: The Col-r/r mouse carries a mutation in the MMP ¾-¼ cleavage site in the triple helical domain of the α1 chain of type I collagen.
source: The Col-r/r mouse carries a mutation in the MMP ¾-¼ cleavage site in the triple helical domain of the α1 chain of type I collagen (Liu et al., 1995) that renders both the α1(I) and α2(I) chains resistant to cleavage by MMPs (Wu et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 1995 and Wu et al., 1990.

claim: The mutation in Col-r/r mice renders both the α1(I) and α2(I) chains resistant to cleavage by MMPs.
source: The Col-r/r mouse carries a mutation in the MMP ¾-¼ cleavage site in the triple helical domain of the α1 chain of type I collagen (Liu et al., 1995) that renders both the α1(I) and α2(I) chains resistant to cleavage by MMPs (Wu et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wu et al., 1990.

claim: There were no significant differences in tendon size between embryonic (E15.5) WT and Col-r/r mice.
source: In contrast to Mmp14 KO, there were no significant differences in tendon size (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A) and collagen fibril diameter (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B) between embryonic (E15.5) WT and Col-r/r mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: There were no significant differences in collagen fibril diameter between embryonic (E15.5) WT and Col-r/r mice.
source: In contrast to Mmp14 KO, there were no significant differences in tendon size (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A) and collagen fibril diameter (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B) between embryonic (E15.5) WT and Col-r/r mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Mmp14 KO and Col-r/r tenocytes have significantly more fibripositor profiles than WT, with Mmp14 KO cells having the most.
source: Analysis of the frequency of fibricarrier profiles per nucleus (using methods used previously [Canty et al., 2006]) showed that Mmp14 KO and Col-r/r tenocytes have significantly more fibripositor profiles than WT, with Mmp14 KO cells having the most (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C, with citation to Canty et al., 2006.

claim: Col-r/r tenocytes contained conspicuous recessed fibripositors, as seen in the Mmp14 KO samples.
source: SBF-SEM analysis showed that Col-r/r tenocytes contained conspicuous recessed fibripositors, as seen in the Mmp14 KO samples (Figure 2C and Video 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C and Video 3.

claim: Electron dense vacuoles were present in Col-r/r tenocytes, which appeared to contain fibrillar structures in various stages of decomposition.
source: Electron dense vacuoles were also present, which appeared to contain fibrillar structures in various stages of decomposition (Figure 2C, white arrows).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Electron dense vacuoles containing fibrillar structures were rarely seen in WT or Mmp14 KO samples.
source: Such compartments were rarely seen in WT or Mmp14 KO samples.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a comparison to Col-r/r samples.

claim: Scx-Cre::Mmp14 lox/lox tendons at P0 contained multiple fibripositors with multiple fibrils, a similar phenotype observed for global Mmp14 KO mice.
source: We examined the tendons at P0 by TEM and confirmed that the Scx-Cre::Mmp14 lox/lox tendons also contained multiple fibripositors with multiple fibrils, a similar phenotype observed for global Mmp14 KO mice (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: At birth the Scx-Cre::Mmp14 lox/lox mice appear normal.
source: At birth the mice appear normal, however, the Scx-Cre::Mmp14 lox/lox mice exhibited a clear limb phenotype ∼1 week after birth, with dorsiflexion of the fore and hind paws (Figure 4C,D, arrowhead) and a dome-shaped skull (Figure 4D, arrow).
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: The Scx-Cre::Mmp14 lox/lox mice exhibited a clear limb phenotype approximately 1 week after birth, with dorsiflexion of the fore and hind paws and a dome-shaped skull.
source: At birth the mice appear normal, however, the Scx-Cre::Mmp14 lox/lox mice exhibited a clear limb phenotype ∼1 week after birth, with dorsiflexion of the fore and hind paws (Figure 4C,D, arrowhead) and a dome-shaped skull (Figure 4D, arrow).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: There was no apparent impairment in movement of tail or back muscles in Scx-Cre::Mmp14 lox/lox mice as observed in Scx-null mice.
source: There was no apparent impairment in movement of tail or back muscles as observed in Scx-null mice (Murchison et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to Murchison et al., 2007.

claim: Difference in size was apparent from 3 weeks postnatal in Scx-Cre::Mmp14 lox/lox mice concurrent with hip dysplasia and reduced bone density.
source: Difference in size was apparent from 3 weeks postnatal concurrent with hip dysplasia and reduced bone density (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), overgrowth of soft tissues in the paws (Figure 4E) and severe dorsiflexion of paws which was particularly obvious in the hind paws (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Scx-Cre::Mmp14 lox/lox mice exhibited overgrowth of soft tissues in the paws.
source: Difference in size was apparent from 3 weeks postnatal concurrent with hip dysplasia and reduced bone density (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), overgrowth of soft tissues in the paws (Figure 4E) and severe dorsiflexion of paws which was particularly obvious in the hind paws (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Scx-Cre::Mmp14 lox/lox mice exhibited severe dorsiflexion of paws which was particularly obvious in the hind paws.
source: Difference in size was apparent from 3 weeks postnatal concurrent with hip dysplasia and reduced bone density (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), overgrowth of soft tissues in the paws (Figure 4E) and severe dorsiflexion of paws which was particularly obvious in the hind paws (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Smaller tendon (tail and Achilles) size and weaker bones were observed in 7-week-old Scx-Cre::Mmp14 lox/lox mice.
source: Smaller tendon (tail and Achilles) size and weaker bones were also observed in 7-week-old Scx-Cre::Mmp14 lox/lox mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: Scx-Cre::Mmp14 lox/lox mice had significantly shorter cranium length and stunted skeletal growth.
source: Morphometric analysis of x-rays confirmed that Scx-Cre::Mmp14 lox/lox mice had significantly shorter cranium length and stunted skeletal growth (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Adult (7 weeks old) WT tendons showed the typical bimodal distribution of collagen fibril diameters.
source: EM analysis of adult (7 weeks old) WT tendons showed the typical bimodal distribution of collagen fibril diameters (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cells in adult (7 weeks old) WT tendons lacked fibripositors and were stellate in cross section.
source: Cells lacked fibripositors and were stellate in cross section (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The tendons of 7-week-old Scx-Cre::Mmp14 lox/lox mice contained a unimodal distribution of small diameter fibrils.
source: In contrast, the tendons of Scx-Cre::Mmp14 lox/lox mice contained a unimodal distribution of small diameter fibrils (Figure 5B), and the cells were engorged with fibrils in membrane-bound compartments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The cells in 7-week-old Scx-Cre::Mmp14 lox/lox tendons were engorged with fibrils in membrane-bound compartments.
source: In contrast, the tendons of Scx-Cre::Mmp14 lox/lox mice contained a unimodal distribution of small diameter fibrils (Figure 5B), and the cells were engorged with fibrils in membrane-bound compartments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cells in 7-week-old Col-r/r tendons were similar in appearance to those in WT tendons.
